title: Parley — AI Agents Negotiate Your Lease via WebMCP
pitch: Two independent AI agents—one for the tenant, one for the landlord—negotiate a real lease renewal live on a shared page, using native WebMCP tools instead of talking to each other directly.
about_excerpt: Two independent AI agents—one for the tenant, one for the landlord—negotiate a real lease renewal live on a shared page, using native WebMCP tools instead of talking to each other directly. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Landing Page of the website How does Parley actually works The 2 Negotiating Agents - Tenant & Landlord agent WebMCP Deal tools used Why I built this Everyone hates negotiating their lease renewal. You either eat the increase or spend hours going back and forth over email. I wanted to see what happens if two AI agents did that instead: one for the tenant and one for the landlord. The catch is my agent and my landlord's agent have no way to talk to each other. WebMCP fixes that. A page exposes structured actions, and any agent, built by anyone, can act on the same shared state through those tools. That's the whole idea behind Parley. What it does A tenant agent and a landlord agent each load the same negotiation page in their own browser session. They never talk directly. All they see is six WebMCP tools: get_negotiation_state propose_terms counter_terms request_concession accept finalize_agreement Every move gets logged as a redline diff—old terms struck through, new terms next to them, like an actual lease amendment. Give each agent a goal and a limit, let them run, and they actually negotiate. Building it Next.js, Firestore for shared state, and document.modelContext.registerTool() for the tools. Both agents read/write the same Firestore doc the UI reads from. No backend glue between them—just the page. The annoying part The WebMCP API changed twice while I was building this. navigator.modelContext got dropped for document.modelContext , and provideContext() got removed entirely, so all context has to live in the tool descriptions now. Bigger issue: my first "successful" test wasn't real. The agent had shell access and just pulled my Firebase key out of the compiled JS and wrote to Firestore directly, skipping the tools completely. Looked fine, proved nothing. Every test after that had to run without terminal access, through the actual browser tool interface, to know it was real. Also, on two separate runs, both agents independently landed on the same sticking point: the tenant kept asking for a smart thermostat, and the landlord kept declining it as outside its budget, while still agreeing on everything else. Nobody scripted that. Real negotiations have exactly one stubborn detail, and mine found it on its own. Proudest part A full negotiation—propose, finalize, six rounds, two agents that never spoke to each other directly—working the same on localhost and on the live deployed site.
